question: A grants officer on a paid plan needs a one-off overview of the funding landscape, drawn from the published criteria of roughly twenty funders she has not looked at before. Her director will ask where each statement came from. Which approach best fits the job?
options: A) Ask a separate question about each of the twenty funders in ordinary chats, then merge the twenty replies into an overview herself.
B) Use Research, which runs the multi-step search across the funders itself and returns an answer with sources she can open and check.
C) Set up a project for the overview, put the twenty funder names into the project instructions and work through them chat by chat.
D) Ask one broad question in an ordinary chat, then ask for a reference list to be added underneath the overview once it is written.
correct_answers: B) Use Research, which runs the multi-step search across the funders itself and returns an answer with sources she can open and check.
explanations: Twenty separate questions is slow, and it puts the entire burden of deciding what to investigate and of stitching the findings together back on the officer, which is the work she wanted help with.

Correct. Research is built for exactly this: an agentic multi-step search across many external sources that decides what to look at next and returns an answer with sources attached, which is what her director's question requires.

A project provides durable shared context for recurring work, but this is a one-off task and the funder criteria are external material she has not gathered. The project adds setup without doing any of the searching.

References requested after the overview is written are assembled to fit text that was produced without them, so they are the weakest form of provenance and still leave every claim to be traced by hand.
